lead: You tap a link and a page appears. Between the tap and the page, three things happen: the browser turns a name into a numeric address, it opens a connection to that address, and it asks for one resource. The name-to-address step is the Domain Name System, or DNS. It exists because people remember names like shop.example.com while routers need numbers like 203.0.113.10. Every UPI payment, every IRCTC ticket check, every video load begins this way. This chapter follows one URL from the browser to the server and back.

sections.h3: The Internet is the road, the web is one kind of traffic

blocks.text: The Internet is a global network of networks. It moves data as packets: small chunks of bytes, each with a header holding a source address and a destination address. An IP address is that number, for example 203.0.113.10. IPv4 addresses are 32 bits, written as four numbers from 0 to 255. IPv6 addresses are 128 bits, written in hexadecimal.
Routers are the machines in between. A router reads the destination address on a packet and forwards it on one of its links. The packet moves hop by hop, and no single machine knows the whole path.

The World Wide Web is a service that runs on the Internet. It is a set of resources, each named by a URL, fetched with HTTP and usually written in HTML. Email, video calls and file transfer also use the Internet but are not the web.

sections.h3: DNS: one name, one address, found by asking in steps

blocks.text: The browser knows a name; the network needs an address. DNS (Domain Name System) is a distributed database that maps names to addresses. No single machine holds every name, so an answer is found by asking a short chain of servers, as the figure shows.

items: The browser asks its configured resolver, usually run by the ISP or a public service.
The resolver asks a root server. The root does not know the address; it refers the resolver to the servers for the top-level domain, here .com.
The resolver asks the TLD (top-level domain) server. It refers the resolver to ns1.example.com, the domain's own authoritative server.
The resolver asks the authoritative server. It answers with the record, for example A 203.0.113.10, plus a TTL.
The resolver returns the answer to the browser and keeps a copy for the TTL.
A record: name to IPv4 address, for example 203.0.113.10.
CNAME record: name to another name, an alias, for example www.example.com to shop.example.com.
MX record: name to a mail server, with a preference number.

blocks.text: TTL (time to live) is the number of seconds a cached answer stays valid. With TTL 300, a resolver may answer from its cache for 300 s and then must ask again. So an answer is held in caches for its TTL and can still change later, once the TTL runs out and a fresh answer is fetched.
A URL (Uniform Resource Locator) names one resource. Take https://shop.example.com:443/items?id=7#top. Each part has one job.

blocks.text: When the port is left out, the scheme supplies it: 80 for http and 443 for https. The query string is sent to the server; the fragment never is.

sections.h3: One URL from tap to page

items: Parse the URL into scheme, host, port, path and query.
Check the browser cache, then the operating system cache, then ask the resolver for the host.
Open a TCP connection to the returned IP address on the port: 443 for https, 80 for http. TLS runs on top of it for https, see 1.4.
Send an HTTP request, for example GET /items?id=7, with a Host header.
The server returns a status code and the resource; see 1.3 for what kind of server answers.
The browser reads the HTML and requests CSS, JavaScript and images, each repeating these steps but usually served from cache.
It builds the page and paints it; the markup and the scripting belong to Unit 2 and Unit 3.

blocks.text: Fetching the main resource is one request-response round trip; the sub-resources the page needs each add their own round trip. Knowing the order tells you where a failure sits: a wrong name is a DNS problem, a refused connection is a port or server problem, a 404 is a path problem.

spec.aria: Browser asks a resolver; the resolver asks the root, the .com TLD server and ns1.example.com in turn, gets 203.0.113.10 with TTL 300 s, and the browser connects to that address on port 443.

examples.question: A browser opens https://shop.example.com:443/items?id=7. Trace the DNS lookup and the connection. State the host, port, path and query. How many servers are asked on the chain, and how long may a cache keep the answer? Which TCP port does the browser use after DNS?
steps: Step 1: split the URL. Scheme is https, host is shop.example.com, port is 443, path is /items, query is id=7. There is no fragment.
Step 2: the browser asks its resolver for shop.example.com.
Step 3: the resolver asks a root server, which refers it to the .com TLD servers. That is server 1.
Step 4: the resolver asks the .com TLD server, which refers it to ns1.example.com. That is server 2.

Step 5: the resolver asks the authoritative server ns1.example.com, which answers A 203.0.113.10 with TTL 300 s. That is server 3. So three name servers were asked on the chain — root, TLD and authoritative — in addition to the browser's own resolver.
Step 6: the resolver caches the record for 300 s, so any cache may answer with 203.0.113.10 for up to 300 s.
Step 7: the scheme is https, so the browser opens a TCP connection to 203.0.113.10 on port 443 and sends GET /items?id=7.
examples.answer: Host shop.example.com, port 443, path /items, query id=7; 3 servers are asked on the chain; the answer may be cached for 300 s; the browser then opens TCP port 443.
examples.check:
url = "https://shop.example.com:443/items?id=7"
rest = url.split("://", 1)[1]
host_port, path_query = rest.split("/", 1)
host, port = host_port.split(":")
path, query = path_query.split("?", 1)
servers_asked = ["root", ".com TLD", "ns1.example.com"]
ttl = 300
print(len(servers_asked))
print(ttl)
print(int(port))

traps: A cached DNS answer skips root, TLD and authoritative servers until the TTL expires. The full walk happens only on a cache miss.

Port 443 is HTTPS and port 80 is HTTP. A URL with no port takes the default from its scheme, so an https URL with no port written means 443 and an http URL with no port means 80. A port written in the URL overrides the default, e.g. https://api.example.org:8443 uses 8443.
The query string (?id=7) is sent to the server; the fragment (#top) is not. Marks are lost by naming the fragment as server data.
A CNAME gives another name, not an address. An MX record points at mail servers, so a domain's mail can live on a different machine from its web site.
The World Wide Web is not the Internet. The web is one service running on the Internet's packet network.

quiz.a: It maps a host name to an IP address, using a distributed set of servers.

quiz.q: Which default ports do http and https use?
quiz.a: http uses port 80; https uses port 443.

quiz.q: Why must the browser resolve the host name before it can connect?
quiz.a: Routers forward packets using IP addresses. The browser has a name, so it needs the numeric address before it can open a TCP connection.

quiz.q: State two differences between the Internet and the World Wide Web.
quiz.a: The Internet is a network of networks that carries packets addressed by IP; the web is a service on it that carries documents named by URL and fetched with HTTP.
Scheme https; host api.example.org; port 8443; path /v2/orders; query page=3; fragment top.

quiz.q: A record has TTL 3600 s and is cached at 10:00. Until when may the cache answer from its copy?
quiz.a: 3600 s is one hour, so the cache may answer until 11:00; after that it must ask the authoritative server again.

quiz.q: Two users open the same site a minute apart. One sees the full DNS walk, the other only one exchange with the resolver. Explain.
quiz.a: The first user's resolver has no valid copy, so it asks root, TLD and authoritative servers and caches the result for the TTL. The second user's resolver still holds that cached answer, so it replies at once. When the TTL expires, the walk repeats.

quiz.q: A domain's web site works but its email fails. Which record type would you inspect first, and why?
quiz.a: The MX record. Web traffic uses the A or AAAA record for the host; mail delivery uses MX, so a wrong or missing MX breaks mail while the site stays up.

beyond: Not for the exam. In production, DNS is also a traffic tool: weighted answers split traffic between servers in set proportions, and latency-based answers send each user to the data centre with the shortest measured delay. Anycast puts one IP address on many machines. DNS over HTTPS encrypts the query inside the connection, so the ISP can see who you are talking to but not which names you asked for. DNSSEC signs answers so a forged reply is rejected. Cloud platforms tie DNS to load balancers, so a host name often points at a service, not a single machine. Search for DNS over HTTPS, DNSSEC, anycast and weighted routing to go further.
